items.stem: In the traditional painter's colour wheel, the primary colours are…
items.explanation: In the RYB model used by painters, red, yellow and blue can't be mixed from other colours and mix to make the rest.

distractors.a: That's the RGB system for light and screens.

items.takeaway: Painters: RYB. Screens: RGB. Printers: CMYK.

items.stem: Mixing blue and yellow paint gives…
items.explanation: Blue + yellow = green, a secondary colour.

items.stem: Red-orange is an example of a…
items.explanation: A tertiary colour mixes a primary with a neighbouring secondary: red + orange = red-orange.

distractors.c: Primaries can't be mixed from others.
distractors.d: Secondaries are orange, green and violet.
distractors.a: Neutrals are greys, beiges and browns.

items.stem: Screens create colours by mixing light. The primary colours of light are…
items.explanation: RGB is additive: red + green + blue light at full strength make white.

items.stem: Why do printers use CMYK instead of RGB?

options.text: RGB inks don't exist in any form
CMYK is cheaper to design with
Inks absorb (subtract) light, so printing mixes subtractively

items.explanation: On paper, inks absorb light; cyan, magenta and yellow subtract red, green and blue. K (black) gives deep blacks and saves ink. Designs for print should be prepared in CMYK.

distractors.a: Screens can show brighter colours than ink.
distractors.b: The reason is how colour mixing works.

items.stem: Colours directly opposite each other on the colour wheel are called…
items.explanation: Complementary pairs (red–green, blue–orange, yellow–violet) create the strongest hue contrast.

distractors.c: That's one hue in different values.
distractors.d: Triadic colours are evenly spaced in threes.

items.stem: Yellow, yellow-green and green together form which harmony?
items.explanation: Neighbouring colours give calm, unified palettes, like a forest or sunset.

distractors.b: That uses a colour plus two near its opposite.

items.stem: Red, yellow and blue used together form which harmony on the RYB wheel?
items.explanation: Three colours equally spaced (120° apart) form a triad: vibrant but balanced.

items.stem: Blue with yellow-orange and red-orange is an example of…
items.explanation: Split-complementary takes a base colour plus the two colours either side of its complement, giving contrast with less tension.

distractors.b: Complementary uses orange itself, not its neighbours.
distractors.c: Blue and the oranges aren't neighbours.

items.stem: A poster using only different tints and shades of blue has a…
items.explanation: Monochromatic schemes are elegant and unified; contrast comes from value rather than hue.

distractors.b: Achromatic means no hue at all.

items.stem: Why do sports teams often use complementary colours on jerseys and logos?

options.text: Maximum contrast makes them stand out and stay readable

items.explanation: Opposite colours intensify each other: energetic and highly visible at a distance.

items.stem: Adding white to a colour creates a…
items.explanation: Pink is a tint of red; sky blue is a tint of blue.

items.stem: Adding black to a colour creates a…
items.explanation: Maroon is a shade of red; navy is a shade of blue.

distractors.a: A complement is the opposite colour.

items.stem: Adding grey to a colour creates a…
items.explanation: Tones are softer, more muted versions: dusty rose, sage green.

items.stem: A design looks great in colour but unreadable when photocopied in black and white. The problem is most likely…

options.text: Not enough value contrast between colours

items.explanation: Colours with similar lightness (like red and green of the same value) turn into the same grey. Check value contrast by viewing in greyscale.

distractors.a: The number of colours isn't the issue.

items.stem: Which group contains only warm colours?
items.explanation: Warm colours remind us of fire and sun; cool colours remind us of water, sky and plants.

items.stem: In landscape paintings, distant mountains are often painted bluish and pale because…

options.text: The atmosphere makes far objects look cooler and lighter (atmospheric perspective)
It's a rule of the RYB wheel

items.explanation: Air scatters light, so distant objects lose contrast and shift towards blue. Using this creates depth.

distractors.d: It's about how we see distance.

items.stem: Warm colours in a room tend to make walls feel…
items.explanation: Warm colours seem to advance and cool colours recede, which interior designers use to change the feel of a space.

items.stem: Which colour is most commonly associated with danger and stopping?
items.explanation: Red is highly visible and linked to urgency, so it's used for stop signs, warnings and emergency buttons.

items.stem: Many banks and tech companies use blue in their logos because blue is often associated with…
items.explanation: Blue feels calm and dependable in many cultures, useful for brands handling money and data.

distractors.d: Reds and oranges are linked to appetite.

items.stem: Why is it risky to show 'correct' and 'wrong' using only green and red?

options.text: Red is too bright for screens
Many colour-blind people can't easily tell red from green

items.explanation: Red–green colour blindness affects roughly 1 in 12 men. Always add a second cue: an icon, a label or a pattern.

items.stem: In many Indian traditions, which colour is associated with weddings and auspicious occasions?
items.explanation: Red (with gold) is traditional for brides in many Indian communities, symbolising prosperity and celebration.

distractors.a: Black is often avoided at weddings.
distractors.b: White is associated with mourning in some traditions.

items.stem: The 'saturation' of a colour describes…

options.text: How light or dark it is
How intense or dull it is

items.explanation: A fully saturated red is vivid; a desaturated red looks greyish.

items.stem: 'Hue' refers to…

options.text: The basic colour family, like red, blue or green

items.explanation: Hue is what we usually mean by 'colour'. Value and saturation then describe its lightness and intensity.

items.stem: Black, white and greys are called…
items.explanation: Achromatic means without hue. They're useful as neutral backgrounds and for testing value.

distractors.c: They have no hue to be opposite.

items.stem: Indigo, a deep blue natural dye used in Indian textiles for centuries, comes from…
items.explanation: India was historically famous for indigo; the word itself comes from 'Indicum', meaning 'from India'.

items.stem: Which spice has traditionally been used as a natural yellow dye?
items.explanation: Turmeric gives a bright but fade-prone yellow, used in rituals, cloth and food colouring.

items.stem: During Holi, colours were traditionally made from…

options.text: Flowers and plants like palash (flame of the forest) and turmeric

items.explanation: Natural colours from flowers, leaves and spices are gentler on skin; many people are returning to them.

distractors.c: These are modern and can be harmful.

items.takeaway: Natural colours are a design opportunity.

items.stem: Many food brands use red and yellow in their logos because these colours are thought to…

options.text: Grab attention and suggest energy and appetite

items.explanation: Warm, high-energy colours are highly visible and linked to quick, cheerful experiences.

distractors.c: Black and gold are more typical for luxury.
distractors.d: Green is more associated with health.

items.stem: A brand palette usually includes…

options.text: One or two primary colours, a few accents and neutrals

items.explanation: A limited, consistent palette makes a brand instantly recognisable across products and media.

distractors.b: Some brands do, but it's not usual.

items.stem: Which pair has the MOST hue contrast?
items.explanation: Blue and orange are complementary, the strongest hue contrast possible.

items.stem: A hospital wants its children's ward to feel calm and safe. Which palette is most suitable?

options.text: Soft blues and greens with warm accents

items.explanation: Soft cool tones calm, while small warm accents keep spaces friendly. Context and users decide colour.
items.takeaway: Colour sets mood: choose for the user.

items.stem: In a pencil drawing, colour is replaced by…
items.explanation: Every colour has a value. Translating colours into the right lightness is the key to strong monochrome drawings.

distractors.d: Texture helps but value carries form.
distractors.a: Line helps but value carries form.
distractors.b: Value still describes light and form.
